draft.title: Environment and interconnection
card: the living and non-living world around us. It includes plants, animals, people, water, soil, air and rock.
the way people, places and processes affect each other. A change in one part can lead to changes in another.
The links can run in both directions. People change environments, and environments shape what people can do and where they live.
Interconnections can join places that are far apart. Water, wind, trade and the movement of people can all carry effects from one place to another.
draft.remember: The environment is everything around us, and interconnection is how its parts affect each other.

opts: Clearing hillside forest raises the silt in a river below
A river is 200 km long and flows towards the east
A farm covers 50 hectares of flat land near a town
A town has a population of 8000 people
a.why: Clearing the forest affects the river, so one part of the environment changes another. The other options only describe a feature of one place and show no effect on anything else.
a.clue: Look for one thing causing a change in another.

b.q: Dust from farmland in western NSW is blown by strong winds and settles on Sydney, lowering air quality there. What does this show?
opts: An interconnection between places far apart, carried by wind
A change that stays inside the farmland environment only
A feature that belongs only to the non-living environment
An effect caused by people with no link to the wind
b.why: A process in one place (wind lifting dust from farmland) affects a distant place, so the places are interconnected. The second option is wrong because the effect reaches Sydney, so it does not stay in the farmland.
b.clue: Ask where the effect starts and where it ends up.

a.best: Clearing hillside forest raises the silt in a river below

b.best: An interconnection between places far apart, carried by wind

problems.detail: The right option echoes the stem and card wording ('far apart', 'wind'). The three wrong options carry giveaway absolutes ('only' twice, 'no link'). A student can pick the answer without understanding interconnection.
Two options use 'only' ('belongs only to the non-living environment', 'stays inside the farmland environment only'), while the card uses open wording such as 'can'.

Why (b) says 'the second option' is wrong because the effect does not stay in the farmland. Options are randomised, and in this order the second option is about the non-living environment. The farmland option is fourth, so the explanation points to the wrong option. It should name the option by its content, not its position.

proposal.title: Environment and interconnection
card: the living and non-living world around us. It includes plants, animals, people, water, soil, air and rock.
the way people, places and processes affect each other. A change in one part can lead to changes in another.
The links can run in both directions. People change environments, and environments shape what people can do and where they live.
Interconnections can join places that are far apart. Water, wind, trade and the movement of people can all carry effects from one place to another.
proposal.remember: Look for the link: a change in one part of the environment or one place can cause a change in another.

opts: Clearing hillside forest raises the silt in a river below
A river is 200 km long and flows towards the east
A farm covers 50 hectares of flat land near a town
A town has a population of 8000 people
a.why: Clearing the forest affects the river, so one part of the environment changes another. The other options describe a feature of one place and show no effect on anything else.
a.clue: Look for one thing causing a change in another.

b.q: Dust lifted from dry farmland in western NSW lowers air quality in Sydney a few days later. Which statement explains the interconnection?
opts: Moving air carries a change in one place to another place
The two places are linked because both are in NSW
Sydney's air is changing the soil on farms to the west
Dust is non-living, so it is not part of the environment
b.why: A process, moving air, carries dust from the farmland to Sydney, so a change in one place affects another. Being in the same state is not what links them: the link is the process that carries the effect. The option saying dust is outside the environment is wrong too, as the environment includes non-living things such as soil and air.
b.clue: Ask what actually travels between the two places.
